Contract-Bound Evidence

Admitting externally-patched open source into a regulated estate

Working draft — 21 July 2026

Abstract

Regulated institutions run large amounts of old, widely-shared open source they cannot upgrade on any useful timescale, because the blocking dependency belongs to someone else. Backpatching — applying a security fix to the version actually in use — is the available bridge, but a backpatch produced by a third party arrives with evidence that party produced about its own work, which is not evidence at all.

This paper describes contract-bound evidence: a model in which the specification is commissioned and countersigned before work begins, and every downstream claim is checked against it by parties who independently re-derived the result. The receiving institution's question moves from did the supplier do good work? — which it cannot answer — to did the output conform to a scope the supplier committed to before starting, independently verified? — which is mechanically decidable.

Two ideas do most of the work. The first is the commissioned specification, which closes the loophole that makes supplier-produced test evidence unfalsifiable. The second is the observation that verification does not compress: unlike proof-of-work, checking a build costs roughly what producing it cost, so a single checker is both a bottleneck and a single point of trust. The response is a quorum of independent verifiers in which disagreement is disqualifying rather than outvoted.

A note on scope

The model is general. It is described here through one instance — OSERA, a FINOS coalition mutualizing the backpatching of old open source across regulated banks — because that instance exists, has named participants, and supplies concrete vocabulary. Nothing in the model depends on OSERA specifically; the same structure applies wherever an organisation must admit code that someone else modified on its behalf, including vendor-maintained forks and internal platform teams patching for downstream business units.

code_tracer is the reference implementation and is named where the distinction between model and implementation matters.

How to read this

Part I is the model and is the part most likely to transfer to other problems. Part II is institutional: commissioning, trust roots, quorum sizing — written for people deciding how an alliance should operate. Part III is what a receiving institution deploys and stores — written for platform and open-source programme teams. Part IV states the limits.

One worked example runs throughout: a deserialization vulnerability in a jackson-databind version pinned by a framework's bill of materials, present transitively across hundreds of applications, where the upgrade is blocked by coupling rather than by effort.

Four figures accompany the text. Figure 1 gives the shape of the system and is worth reading before Part I; the rest appear where they are relevant.

Part I — The model

1. The bind

Start with the situation as it actually presents, rather than as a policy document imagines it.

A bank runs several hundred applications. Somewhere in their dependency trees — typically three or four levels down, arriving transitively through a framework's bill of materials — sits a version of jackson-databind. No team chose it. No team can tell you why that version rather than another. It is there because the framework's dependency management put it there, and it has been there for years.

A deserialization vulnerability is published against it.

The remediation is obvious and unavailable. The fix exists upstream, in a later release. Adopting that release means moving the framework BOM that pins it, which means a coordinated upgrade across a release train no single application team controls, scheduled against a change calendar that has other commitments. The honest estimate is quarters, not weeks. Meanwhile the scanner fires on every application in the estate, and the risk function has an exposure it cannot close and cannot explain away.

This is the bind, and it is worth being precise about its shape:

  • The exposure is broad, because the library is shared.
  • The upgrade is blocked by coupling, not by effort. This distinction matters. A blocked-by-effort problem is a resourcing conversation. A blocked-by-coupling problem cannot be solved by the party that has the problem.
  • The window is long, and it is measured in the calendar of whoever owns the blocking dependency.

The available response is a backpatch: take the version the estate actually runs, apply the security fix to it, ship a hardened build under a distinct coordinate. This is not a new technique. What it lacks, when done ad hoc, is any basis on which a regulated institution can admit the result.

Three properties make a backpatch bearable rather than reckless. First, it is deliberately temporary — a bridge to an upstream fix that will eventually be adoptable, carrying a sunset date, because a privately-maintained fork is itself a standing liability. Second, it is narrow: fix only, no features, no drift, and provable API/ABI stability, because the whole value is that it drops into a running estate without a code change. Third, and the subject of this paper, it must arrive with evidence a machine can check.

Backpatching is also expensive and, done per-institution, absurdly duplicative: every bank in the sector fixing the same library in parallel, each producing evidence only it trusts. Mutualizing the work across an alliance is the obvious efficiency. It is also what creates the problem the rest of this paper solves. The moment the patch is produced by someone else, the receiving institution's question changes from did we do this correctly? to why should we believe they did?

2. Why provider-produced evidence is not evidence

The natural response is to ask the provider for proof. Publish the SBOM, the test results, the vulnerability analysis, the build provenance — sign all of it, attach it to the artifact, let the consumer verify the signatures.

This is better than nothing and it is not sufficient, for a reason that has nothing to do with anyone's honesty.

The party producing the evidence is the party being evaluated. The provider selects what to test, runs the tests, interprets the results, and signs the report. Every artifact in that chain is authentic — correctly signed, untampered, verifiable. And the chain establishes only that the provider said these things, not that they are true.

The sharpest form of the problem is the test corpus. Consider the claim all tests passed. If the corpus was chosen after the patch was written — after someone could observe which tests the patch happens to pass — then the claim is unfalsifiable. It is not a lie. It is a statement with no fixed referent, and it will survive any amount of cryptographic verification, because signatures attest to authorship rather than to adequacy.

The same structure recurs at every level. These CVEs are fixed — as assessed by whom, against what scope? No regressions — against which baseline? Coverage meets threshold — measured over which code, chosen when?

Signing solves tampering. It does not solve self-assessment. Any design that treats a signed provider claim as evidence has simply relocated the trust relationship into a cryptographic envelope and declared the problem handled.

Two moves fix this, and the rest of Part I is those two moves.

3. Commissioned specification

The first move: fix the specification before the work starts, and have the provider countersign it.

The alliance issues a contract. It names, by content digest rather than by version string:

  • the baseline — the exact upstream artifact to start from;
  • the scope — which CVEs must be fixed, and, explicitly, which present-but- unfixed CVEs are out of scope;
  • the test corpus — named by digest, so it cannot be substituted;
  • the thresholds — API/ABI stability required, patched-path coverage minimum;
  • the schedule — delivery window, and the sunset date of the resulting bridge.

The provider countersigns before beginning. From that moment the deliverable is a commissioned specification rather than a post-hoc submission, and the corpus loophole closes: all required tests passed now has a fixed referent that was frozen before anyone could see which tests would be convenient.

This is a small mechanical change with a large epistemic consequence. The question the receiving institution asks moves from did the provider do good work? — a judgement it is not positioned to make — to did the output conform to a scope the provider committed to before starting? The second question has a mechanical answer.

Everything downstream is checked against this contract rather than for internal consistency. It is not a document that sits beside the evidence; it is the referent every piece of evidence points back to. We call it L-1, the layer beneath the chain, because the chain is verified relative to it.

Two properties of the contract matter later. It is frozen at countersignature — any change is a new version with a new digest and a fresh signature, carrying an explicit supersession pointer, so the audit trail records what changed and when. And it is machine-readable by construction, because it will be compiled, not read: a deterministic transform emits the verification policy that the receiving institution's gate enforces. One authored artifact, two representations, the same digest lineage. No human reads a PDF and forms an opinion.

4. The chain and the anchor

Above L-1 sits the evidence chain proper. In the OSERA instance it has ten levels — baseline, vulnerability assessment, transformation, build provenance, test results, vulnerability proof, SBOM and diff, VEX, verification summary, acceptance — but the level count is not the interesting part, and a reader who memorizes it has learned the least transportable thing in this paper.

Three principles do the work.

Everything is digest-bound. No attestation refers to a version string. Subjects are content digests plus a package URL. Version strings are metadata; they are labels for humans and dependency resolvers, never identity. This is what makes the graph checkable rather than merely readable.

Every link names both artifacts. Each attestation carries both the baseline digest and the hardened digest. A claim that names only one is unverifiable — you cannot check this fixes that against a statement that mentions only this — and must be rejected outright rather than accepted with reservations.

The chain is a directed graph, not a list. Each attestation references its inputs by digest, so the graph is traversable from the deployed artifact back to the upstream commit, and the traversal is enforced rather than documented.

Then there is the property everything else rests on, and it is the one most likely to be quietly wrong.

The anchor must be independently observable. The first link — this is the upstream artifact and source commit we started from — is a self-claim. If the provider merely asserts it, the entire structure is a self-claim with nine extra steps and considerably better production values. It is load-bearing only if it can be re-derived from public data by a party with no relationship to the provider: the baseline digest must match the artifact publicly retrievable from the ecosystem's own registry at the stated coordinates, and the source reference must be a real commit in the public upstream repository. The verifier re-pulls and compares. No trust is required, and none is extended.

For our example this holds strongly. jackson-databind lives in Maven Central, which is immutable and permits no unpublishing, so the artifact at these coordinates has this digest is a durable, independently checkable fact. Not every ecosystem gives this for free, and Part IV returns to what changes when it does not — the strength of the anchor turns out to determine which ecosystems this model can support at all.

5. Verification does not compress

The second move is the one with the widest application beyond this domain, and it begins with an analogy that fails instructively.

The situation resembles a problem distributed systems has thought about carefully: parties who cannot fully trust each other need to agree on a fact. Something transplants from that literature, and something crucial does not.

What transplants: verify, don't trust, and the observation that deterministic processes let any party re-derive an answer independently. If a build is reproducible — bit-for-bit identical given identical inputs — then any party with the inputs can rebuild and compare digests, and agreement is a matter of arithmetic rather than authority.

What does not transplant: consensus machinery. There is no double-spend problem here, no scarce resource being allocated, and the alliance is a legitimately trusted neutral venue rather than an adversarial anonymous network. A consensus protocol would solve a problem this domain does not have while adding latency a release SLA cannot absorb. Hash-linked, append-only, tamper-evident logs: yes, unreservedly. Distributed consensus, canonical-chain agreement, tokens: no, and the distinction is worth stating plainly because the vocabulary invites conflation.

Now the failure of the analogy, which is where the design turns.

In proof-of-work, the asymmetry is the entire point: work is expensive to produce and cheap to verify. Anyone can check a hash in microseconds. That asymmetry is what lets a network converge cheaply.

Here there is no asymmetry. Verification does not compress. Reproducing a build and re-running a test suite costs approximately what producing it cost. A verifier is not a cheap checker; it is a second provider doing the same work and comparing notes.

Two consequences follow, and they point in the same direction.

First, a single verifier is a throughput bottleneck — it must do the full work of production for every artifact in the pipeline.

Second, and more seriously, a single verifier is a single point of trust. Separating provider from checker hardens the design against provider compromise and does exactly nothing about checker compromise. Compromise one verifier's signing keys or build infrastructure and the entire model collapses in one move — with the receiving institutions seeing a perfectly valid signature over a perfectly false claim.

The fix is a quorum, not a chain. Because reproducible builds are deterministic, independent verifiers converge on the same digest without coordinating. There is no protocol between them, no messages, no leader. The correct answer is a natural focal point — the one result every honest party independently arrives at — and agreement is an artifact of determinism rather than of negotiation. Each verifier publishes its own signed verification summary, and admission requires the whole set to agree.

The most important design decision in this paper is what happens when they disagree.

Dissent is disqualifying, not outvoted. If five institutions rebuild and four agree while one produces a different digest, the honest reading is not four against one. It is that something is wrong — either the toolchain specification is underdetermined and the build is not as reproducible as claimed, or something considerably worse — and either way the receiving institutions need to know loudly, before promotion. So the rule is unanimity across the verifier set, never a simple majority. A dissenting verification summary triggers investigation, not arithmetic.

This inverts the usual instinct. Majority voting is designed to tolerate disagreement and produce an answer anyway. Here, disagreement is the most valuable signal the system can generate, and a design that averages it away has discarded its own best alarm. It is also a signal no single-checker design can produce at all — with one verifier there is nothing to disagree with — and that, more than throughput or redundancy, is the strongest argument for the quorum.

Two practical notes. Who sits in that set, and how large it needs to be, is settled in Part II: the short version is that verification binds to the parties that sign and fund the contract, so the set is named rather than sized. And that set is frozen into the contract at issuance, so an artifact is judged against the parties who committed to it rather than against a membership that drifted afterwards.

One further reproduction happens later and matters more than its position suggests: the institution that adopts the package rebuilds it again, inside its own perimeter, before admitting it. Part III describes where that sits and why it is what makes the whole arrangement work for a package only one institution commissioned.

Part I establishes the model: commission the specification before the work, anchor it in publicly observable fact, and require independent reproduction with zero dissent. Part II turns to who commissions, who verifies, and how the trust root survives the parties that hold it. Part III is what a receiving institution actually deploys.

Part II — Commissioning and trust

Part I described the model. This part is about the institutional machinery underneath it: who decides what gets commissioned, who checks the result, what happens when a commitment is not met, and how the trust root survives the organisations that hold it. These are governance questions, and they are the ones an alliance has to settle before any of the engineering matters.

6. Issuance, and what happens when delivery falls short

The contract has its own lifecycle, separate from the artifact's. It is drafted, proposed to the provider, accepted when the provider countersigns, delivered, and finally fulfilled when the verifiers confirm conformance. It can also be withdrawn before acceptance, breached on delivery, or lapse if the delivery window passes with nothing produced.

Acceptance is the hinge. Before it, the draft is mutable and internal to the issuer. From it, scope, baseline, corpus and thresholds are frozen and signed, and the artifact lifecycle begins. Everything Part I claims about commissioned specification rests on that one transition being clean.

The hand-off at delivery deserves a note, because it closes a loophole one layer out from the corpus problem. The provider assembles a delivery manifest — the contract plus its own attestations — and its digest is written to a transparency log. This establishes that this exact set existed at this time, and it stops the provider adjusting the submission after seeing how verification went. Deliberately, the freeze is a log entry rather than a signature: an inclusion proof cannot be misread as anyone's endorsement of the contents.

Conformance is binary

Verification reports conformance as full, partial, or breach. Only full admits. Partial and breach never promote, under any circumstance.

This looks harsh, and working groups reliably propose softening it: surely a backpatch that fixes four of five commissioned CVEs is better than nothing, and surely the receiving institution should be allowed to weigh that for itself.

The argument against is that a discretionary middle state destroys the property the contract was created to establish. Once partial can promote, someone has to decide which partials are acceptable — and that decision is exactly the unstructured judgement the commissioned specification removed. It also puts the decision in the wrong place: the receiving institution's gate would be adjudicating whether the alliance's commissioning was met, artifact by artifact. And the contract is on a trajectory toward executable terms, where a discretionary state has no representation at all.

An honest shortfall routes through amendment. If a fifth CVE proves unfixable, the contract is amended: that CVE moves to the explicitly-out-of-scope list with a stated reason, the provider countersigns the new version, and delivery is then full against a contract that tells the truth. The residual exposure is recorded in a signed document that the receiving institution can read, rather than buried inside a softened verdict.

This is the better outcome for the same reason double-entry bookkeeping beats a fudge: the shortfall becomes visible and attributable instead of absorbed. The cost is process friction — an amendment cycle takes days that a verdict override would take minutes — and that friction is the mechanism working.

Amendments are versions of the same commitment, carrying an explicit supersession pointer, so the record shows what changed and when. This is distinct from renewal, which produces a new commitment in the same lineage when a bridge expires. Collapsing the two would lose the distinction between "we changed what we asked for" and "we asked again, later."

7. A trust root that outlives its holders

Everything in the model reduces to a question of key management: which signatures does the receiving institution's gate accept, and who decides?

The naive answer is that the alliance holds the root key. This fails on continuity. Alliances form, merge, restructure and dissolve. If the root sits with a single organisation, then every artifact ever admitted becomes unverifiable the moment that organisation ceases to exist — not because anything was wrong with the artifacts, but because the trust material can no longer be re-signed. Root metadata carries an expiry, so this is a scheduled failure rather than a hypothetical one.

So the root is co-signed by a threshold of parties spanning the alliance and its member institutions. Re-signing requires k of m, so it survives any single party disappearing, and no single compromised key can rotate the root. This is the same shape as verification, applied to trust material — the design uses thresholds wherever a single key would otherwise be load-bearing.

Bilateral work needs a delegated namespace

Not all work is commissioned collectively. An institution may contract a provider directly, for a library only it cares about. That work should not be signed under the alliance's root, because the alliance did not commission it and cannot stand behind the judgement.

The established mechanism handles this: delegation. The root delegates a namespace to a named institution, which signs its own bilateral work. The delegation is visible in the trust metadata, so a receiving institution can see which path an artifact arrived by. Importantly, a delegate cannot sign a new root, which keeps the blast radius of a compromised delegation contained.

No weaker tier

The tempting design here is a tiered one: artifacts over the alliance root get full trust, delegated artifacts get a reduced check or an extra approval step.

That would be a mistake, and the reason is worth stating plainly. The admission rules verify properties of the artifact and its evidence: that the baseline anchors publicly, that the proofs hold, that independent parties re-derived the result. None of those properties depend on who commissioned the work. A tier system would therefore either apply a check that adds nothing, or relax one that mattered — and relaxing it would mean the strict version was never necessary.

The trust path is recorded on the verdict for attribution. It tells you who stood behind the commissioning judgement, which is genuinely useful when something goes wrong. It does not alter what the gate requires.

One honest qualification, developed in §8: the rules are identical across paths, and so is the work the receiving institution does. What varies is how many independent reproductions accompanied the artifact before it arrived.

The related decision concerns the transparency log. A shared log operated by the alliance is convenient, but a log operator can in principle present different views to different parties. Rather than adding a separate witness network, each verifier records the log state it observed at the time of verification, and those observations travel with the evidence. Agreement across the verifiers makes a split view detectable, using machinery already present for other reasons.

8. Who verifies, and how many

The unresolved question in early drafts was what motivates an institution to verify someone else's artifact. The first answer was to make verification a credit — count it against membership dues, so institutions that verify pay less.

That answer collapses on contact with bilateral commissioning. If verification earns credit and an institution can commission alone, the rational strategy is to commission solo and never verify, which starves the verifier pool precisely when it is needed. Worse, the institutions most able to verify are the ones most able to go it alone.

The second answer was to make verification an obligation of membership: members verify what the alliance commissions, and the cost is a CI job. That works, and it has an awkward edge — it conscripts institutions into checking projects they neither asked for nor consume, and it leaves unanswered which member checks which project.

The answer the model settles on is that verification follows the money. The institutions that sign and fund a contract are the institutions that verify it. All of them verify, all must agree, and a collectively-commissioned project needs at least two signatories to exist at all.

The argument is that financial exposure is a firmer binding than an obligation. A signatory has already accepted the cost, and it will run the result in its own estate, so it carries the consequence of a bad patch twice over. It also disposes of the assignment problem: there is no rule needed for who checks what, because the contract already names them, and no project can stall waiting for a volunteer.

The cost is a sunk-cost pull in the other direction — a funder that needs the package in production has some motive to see it pass. What holds the line is that the comparison is digest equality, with nothing to interpret or soften.

How many is enough

Earlier drafts set a floor of three, justified on the grounds that two verifiers disagreeing give no way to tell which is wrong without a third.

That justification does not survive inspection, because nothing in this design arbitrates. Disagreement is disqualifying rather than resolvable: two agree and the package admits, two disagree and it stops, and five would behave the same way. The third verifier was never going to break a tie, because there are no ties to break.

What two rather than three does cost is compromise resistance — one bad signer is half the outside evidence rather than a third of it. That is accepted, and the reason it is acceptable is the next section.

The receiving institution verifies too

The strongest reproduction in the model is the one nobody commissioned.

Every adopting institution rebuilds the package itself, from source and toolchain references pinned by digest in the evidence, and signs its own verification summary. This happens while it is still online, during resolution, before the evidence is sealed for offline verification — so the gate still decides from a sealed bundle and the decision is still replayable.

This is what makes a solo-commissioned artifact consumable without a weaker tier. A solo project has one signatory and therefore one reproduction before the perimeter; the maker and the checker are separated at the point where the decision is made by the institution taking the risk. And it is why a revoked verifier key does not unravel past admissions: whatever happened outside, the receiving institution had rebuilt the package for itself.

The honest cost is that verification does not compress for consumers either. Each adopting institution pays roughly production cost per package. Sampling would reduce it and would make the work differ by commissioning mode, which is the distinction this design refuses to draw.

The threshold in force is frozen into the contract at issuance, along with the signatory set. An artifact is judged against the parties who committed to it when it was commissioned, rather than against a set that drifted during the work.

One consequence has to be stated because it affects formation planning: a collectively-commissioned project cannot begin until a second institution will co-fund it. Co-funding is therefore a launch prerequisite, and an alliance that signs a provider before it has members willing to pair up will have commissioned work under contracts that cannot reach fulfilment.

Part II settles the institutional questions: a commitment that freezes on countersignature, a shortfall that surfaces as an amended contract, a trust root that survives its holders, and verification bound to the parties that pay for the work and then rebuilt again by whoever adopts it. Part III is what a receiving institution deploys.

Part III — Admission and afterlife

Parts I and II described a model and who operates it. This part is about what a receiving institution actually runs, what it stores, and what it is still on the hook for a year later. The short version is that the gate is smaller than people expect and the afterlife is larger.

9. The contract compiles to a policy

The L-1 contract is machine-readable for a specific reason: it is compiled, not read. A deterministic transform turns the signed contract into the verification policy the gate enforces. One authored artifact, two representations.

This matters because the alternative — a human reading a contract and configuring a gate to match — reintroduces exactly the gap the contract was written to close. An operator who mistypes a threshold, or who configures last quarter's scope, produces a gate that passes artifacts the contract would have rejected, and nothing in the system notices.

Both sides compile, and the digests must agree. The issuer compiles the policy and distributes it. The receiving institution recompiles it locally from the same signed contract and compares digests. A mismatch is a failed admission.

The temptation is to skip this: the issuer signs the compiled policy, so why not just verify the signature? Because a signature establishes authorship, not correctness. Accepting a signed policy without recompiling inserts a trusted compiler into a design whose entire premise is that you verify rather than trust. Recompilation costs milliseconds and removes a component from the trusted set — one of the better trades in the design. It does impose a real engineering constraint: the compiler must be byte-deterministic, which means no timestamps, no map iteration order, no environment leakage. The compiler version travels with the policy so that a version skew surfaces as a digest mismatch rather than as silent divergence.

Structure and meaning are different checks

Verification runs in two passes, and the split is not arbitrary.

The structural pass asks whether the right steps ran, in the right order, signed by the right parties, with the graph intact and thresholds met. It is a graph and signature check. It knows nothing about vulnerabilities.

The semantic pass asks whether the evidence means what the contract requires: that the CVEs proven fixed cover the commissioned scope, that the test corpus matched by digest, that coverage cleared its threshold, that conformance is FULL, and that each vulnerability record the scope cites still reads as it did when the work was commissioned.

That last check deserves a note, because it closes the final place the contract rested on an author's claim. The affected-version range written into the scope is written by whoever drafts the contract, and nothing checked it against the advisory it cites. So the advisory record is pinned at commissioning and travels inside the evidence, and the gate confirms the range the contract asserts against the copy that was frozen. Verification runs against that copy rather than the live feed on purpose: advisory records legitimately move, a range widened six months later is enrichment working correctly, and gating on it would refuse a conforming artifact over something the provider never controlled. Drift since commissioning belongs to the ledger as an exposure finding.

Keeping the two passes separate has a practical payoff. The structural layer is a mature, general-purpose framework that this design consumes unmodified. The semantic layer is a policy file — readable, reviewable, diffable, and modifiable by a security engineer without touching verification machinery. When a bank's risk function asks what exactly does the gate check?, the answer is a file they can read, not a codebase they have to trust.

For the running example: the structural pass confirms that a rebuild step ran and was signed by three registered verifiers. The semantic pass confirms that the deserialization CVE named in the contract has a proof that fails on the baseline jackson-databind and passes on the hardened one, and that the corpus those results came from is the corpus the contract named.

10. The perimeter

Because verification is hermetic and offline, the boundary crossing cannot be a protocol. There is no live call to the alliance at verification time. What crosses is a copy of a self-contained, content-addressed set of files — the evidence bundle.

This produces the design test the whole interface is built around: if the gate needs it, it ships in the bundle. Anything the gate would have to fetch is a live dependency, and a live dependency means the decision cannot be replayed later from stored inputs. Every admission rule must be decidable from bundle contents alone; a rule that isn't is either a wrong rule or a missing bundle element.

It arrives in two parts, assembled by two parties. The alliance seals an evidence core once per fulfilled contract — the provider's attestations, the verifiers' summaries, the signed contract, the compiled policy, and a pinned copy of each vulnerability record the scope cites. None of that ages, so the core carries no expiry and can be cited years later. The receiving institution then wraps it in an ingest envelope holding what is needed to judge those signatures today: a trust-root snapshot, log checkpoints, certificate roots, and where the artifact sits locally.

The split earns its cost in a single property. The core has one digest, identical for every institution that receives it, so two of them can establish that they admitted the same evidence — a comparison that assembling per-institution would make impossible, since it would produce as many identifiers as recipients over one set of facts. It also puts each clock where it belongs: the evidence has none, and the material used to judge it is refreshed locally on a schedule.

Sealing confers no authority. Neither part carries a signature of its own, and packaging evidence establishes nothing about it — every element inside is independently signed and independently verified. This keeps assembly from becoming a trust role: the party that packages the evidence gains no power over whether it is believed, which is what allows the envelope to be assembled inside the receiving institution without anyone having to vouch for the assembler. One engineering consequence follows directly, because the pinned advisory records are digested exactly as they are carried: assembly must preserve those bytes verbatim, with no reformatting or re-encoding in any transport form.

Resolution is online; verification is offline. Discovering which attestations belong to an artifact digest requires a lookup, and that lookup happens before the bundle is sealed. Once sealed, nothing else is consulted. The perimeter is that line, not the institution's firewall. This distinction is what allows a central discovery index to exist without compromising hermeticity: the index is a lookup rather than evidence, no admission rule depends on it, and a wrong answer fails immediately against signed, digest-bound attestations.

Offline verification forfeits freshness, which has to be handled explicitly. A trust-root snapshot pinned into a bundle cannot learn that a verifier key was revoked yesterday. So the envelope carries stated maximum ages — a longer clock for the trust root, a much shorter one for transparency-log checkpoints — and exceeding either is a named-rule rejection, not a warning. A warning defers the decision to whoever is reading the console, which is not a control. Re-resolution is cheap, because only the trust material needs refreshing; the core and the artifact are unchanged.

What you actually deploy

This is the part most likely to surprise a platform team, and it is the strongest adoption argument in the model.

The gate is a CI job. It invokes a general-purpose attestation verifier for the structural pass and a policy engine for the semantic pass. Most regulated institutions already run both — the policy engine is frequently already deployed for Kubernetes admission control. The gate is stateless: it reads a bundle and writes a verdict.

The storage is unremarkable. A quarantine repository for arriving packages, which nothing but the gate may read. A registry for bundles. A directory of trust material — a trust-root snapshot, certificate roots, checkpoints, the schema and policy the bundle pinned — refreshed on a schedule under ordinary configuration management, not a service. An append-only ledger. The existing repository manager serves as the golden repository, unchanged.

The one-reader rule on quarantine is a control, not a convenience. If any other system can read the quarantine repository, an application team can consume an unadmitted artifact by pointing at the wrong repository, and every guarantee in this paper evaporates without a single check failing.

What is genuinely new is short: the contract-to-policy compiler, the semantic policy itself, the resolver that assembles bundles, the harness that runs the institution's own acceptance tests as a verification step, and the ledger. That is a small surface, and none of it is exotic infrastructure.

The institution's own tests are not optional. They run inside the gate, as a verification step whose result folds into the admit-or-reject decision rather than as a separate downstream stage. The reasoning is uncomfortable but sound: under a warranty-free distribution model, nobody is contractually answerable when a conforming backpatch nonetheless breaks production. A conforming artifact is not the same as a compatible one, and compatibility with a particular estate is the one thing the alliance cannot test on anyone's behalf. This step never leaves the institution and is never shared.

11. Bridges expire

Admission is the beginning of the obligation, not the end of it. A backpatch is deliberately temporary — a bridge to an upstream fix that will eventually be adoptable. An institution that admits bridges without tracking their expiry has replaced a known vulnerability with an unmanaged dependency on a third party's continued goodwill, which is not obviously an improvement.

So the ledger is not a reporting nicety. It is the half of the system the risk function touches daily, and it answers a question the gate cannot: what are we running now, what does it cover, and when does it lapse?

The ledger is an append-only, hash-chained event log, with everything else computed from it. Events record issuance, renewal, expiry, retirement, and verifier revocation. Current state is a projection replayed from the chain rather than a stored row.

The reason is an audit question that a last-write-wins table cannot answer: which bridge was in force in March, and exactly which CVEs did it cover? A mutable status column knows only the present. An event chain replays to any past date. Since the entire model exists to make regulatory claims defensible, storing the operational half in a form that forgets its own history would be a strange place to economize. The chaining also makes tampering detectable — break one link and the whole tail is invalid — which is the same discipline the attestation chain uses, applied to the institution's own records.

One consequence worth stating: "expiring soon" is computed, never stored. Deriving it from the expiry date and a warning window avoids a mutable status that would need its own writer and its own clock, and therefore its own failure mode.

Renewal is a new artifact, not a status change

When a bridge approaches expiry and upstream still isn't adoptable, the response is a renewal — and a renewal is a new package that supersedes the old one, not a date extension on the existing one.

This is not bookkeeping pedantry. The second bridge has its own commissioned contract, its own baseline, and very often a different CVE set — for a library with recurring deserialization issues, bridge two typically closes vulnerabilities that did not exist when bridge one was commissioned. Treating that as "the same bridge, extended" would erase precisely the information the ledger exists to retain. The two are linked by an explicit supersession pointer and share a stable lineage key, so the chain is traversable while each link remains distinct.

Revocation records an exposure; it does not invalidate

When a verifier's key is revoked, what happens to the artifacts admitted on that verifier's summaries?

They stay admitted. Admission was valid at the time, against a pinned trust-root version, and the artifacts themselves are unchanged — they still rebuild to the same digest and still prove the same vulnerabilities fixed. The event is recorded against every affected lineage, and the console raises a review trigger for the risk function to judge case by case.

The alternative is worse than it first appears. Automatically invalidating everything a revoked key touched would let a single trust event pull hundreds of packages out of production simultaneously — a self-inflicted outage triggered by key hygiene rather than by any defect in an artifact. This is tolerable precisely because of the zero-dissent quorum: with a floor of three independent verifiers and no disagreement permitted, no single verifier was ever the sole basis for an admission.

The console writes nothing durable. It is a read tier over projections and verdicts. Every state change routes through the gate, which writes a verdict, or the ledger, which appends an event. This is what keeps the audit trail complete: there is no path by which someone clicks a button and changes the record.

12. Which ecosystems this works for

The model is ecosystem-agnostic in principle and constrained in practice, and the constraint sits in two places that are easy to miss.

Anchor strength varies. The first link in the chain is only load-bearing if the baseline can be re-pulled from a registry nobody in the alliance controls. Some registries are immutable and permit no unpublishing, so the artifact at these coordinates has this digest is durable. Go goes further, publishing an independent checksum log that is stronger than anything this design constructs by hand. But npm and PyPI permit deletion, which means a baseline can vanish after the fact and the anchor check becomes unrepeatable. Those ecosystems need a supplementary witness recorded at commissioning, so that this digest was the published artifact at time T survives removal.

Reproducibility gates feasibility. Independent verification requires that rebuilds converge bit-for-bit. This is workable in the Java ecosystem, good in Go and Rust, and materially harder in npm and Python, where builds routinely embed timestamps, absolute paths, and platform detail. Without reproducibility there is no digest agreement, therefore no quorum, therefore no admission. Ecosystem support is a feasibility question, not a sequencing preference — an ecosystem is supportable when its builds can be made reproducible, and not before. Stating this plainly avoids promising support the verification model cannot deliver.

There is a third constraint, smaller but sharp. The hardened artifact needs a coordinate that sorts above its baseline in the ecosystem's own version ordering, never collides with a real upstream release, and increases across renewals. In Maven's version grammar a qualifier suffix satisfies this. Under PEP 440, a local version identifier does. Under semver, neither form works: a pre-release suffix sorts below the base version — so a resolver would treat the hardened artifact as older than the vulnerable one it replaces — and build metadata is ignored for precedence entirely. That is an open problem, and it may constrain which ecosystems are viable regardless of reproducibility.

Adding an ecosystem is therefore a deliberate act with four prerequisites: an anchor class, reproducible builds, a valid coordinate encoding, and a way to carry attestations.

Part III is the deployable half: a compiled policy, a bundle that crosses once, a gate built largely from software the institution already runs, and a ledger that outlives the admission decision by design. Part IV is what the model does not do.

Part IV — Limits

13. What this model does not do

A design paper that lists only its strengths is asking to be believed rather than checked. This part states the limits plainly. Some are open problems that further work could close; two are structural, and no amount of engineering will remove them.

A faithful build of a malicious change passes every check

This is the sharpest limit, and it follows directly from what reproducibility proves.

Independent rebuild establishes that the artifact corresponds to the stated inputs: this source, this transformation, this toolchain, producing exactly these bytes. Every verifier confirming the same digest confirms that the provider's described change was applied faithfully and that nothing else was introduced during the build.

It says nothing about whether the change itself is benign. A provider who inserts a backdoor into the declared transformation produces an artifact that rebuilds identically for every verifier, passes the vulnerability proofs, passes the test corpus, and conforms perfectly to the contract. The quorum will agree, correctly, that this is what the recipe produces.

The model therefore shifts the trust question rather than eliminating it: from did the provider test adequately? — which it answers well — to is the provider acting in good faith? — which it does not address at all. Source review of the transformation remains a separate control, and the contract's requirement that the recipe set be content-addressed exists to make that review possible and repeatable. An alliance that treats independent verification as a substitute for looking at the patch has misread what the verification proves.

Verifiers may fail in correlated ways

The quorum assumes independence. In practice, verifiers are likely to run similar toolchains, similar container images, and a shared rebuild harness distributed by the alliance — because that is the cheapest way to make verification a low-effort membership obligation.

A defect in that shared harness is a common-mode failure. Every verifier could converge on the same wrong answer with no dissent, which is exactly the signal the design relies on to detect trouble. The mitigation is partial: encourage diversity in build environments, and treat the harness as security-relevant code in its own right. But the tension is real, and it runs against the operational pressure to standardise.

The quorum verifies conformance, not judgement

Verification confirms that delivery matched the contract. Nobody independently checks that the contract asked for the right things.

If the commissioned scope omits a CVE that mattered, or names a test corpus too weak to catch a regression, every downstream check will pass and the artifact will be admitted. The scope decision sits with the issuer and, in solo mode, with a single institution. That decision is recorded and attributable — the governance block makes it checkable after the fact — but it is not verified by anyone before the work proceeds.

Open problems

Version coordinates in semver ecosystems. The hardened artifact needs a coordinate sorting above its baseline. Under semver, a pre-release suffix sorts below the base version and build metadata is ignored for precedence, so neither available form works. Until this is resolved, npm and cargo cannot be supported even where reproducibility is achievable.

Schema compatibility over time. Signed contracts are frozen permanently and the ledger must answer questions about them years later, so the gate has to evaluate every schema version ever issued. Nothing can be deprecated. The versioning and compatibility rules for that schema are unspecified, and the problem only becomes visible once both sides ship independently.

Anchor durability in deletion-permitting registries. npm and PyPI allow unpublishing, so a baseline can disappear after commissioning and the anchor check becomes unrepeatable. The proposed remedy — recording a log witness at commissioning — is sound but adds a step that must actually be performed, at the moment when nobody yet has a reason to care.

Reconciliation of the discovery index. The central attestation index is rebuildable from the transparency log, which is what makes omission detectable rather than silent. Detectable, however, only if someone performs the reconciliation. The operating model proposes an owner and a daily cadence, with the resulting lag published as a figure so the distance between log and index is visible rather than assumed. Neither the owner nor the interval is settled, and until they are this is a duty nobody holds — which is the failure mode the whole class of standing obligations shares: nothing rejects, nothing alarms, and the omission surfaces only when a package cannot be discovered.

Governance policy. Who sits in the trust-root threshold, how verifiers are admitted and removed, and what happens on suspected compromise are undecided. These are the largest remaining items and they are not engineering questions.

Two things the model deliberately does not attempt

It is not a substitute for upgrading. Every bridge carries an expiry, and the ledger exists to make expiry impossible to ignore. An institution that renews indefinitely has built a permanent private fork with extra ceremony, which is a worse position than the one it started from — the model can make that visible, but it cannot prevent it.

It offers no warranty. A neutral venue distributing hardened open source will not warrant fitness, and nobody is contractually answerable when a conforming backpatch breaks production. The contract narrows what has to be accepted on faith — as-is, but provably conforming to a scope committed in advance and independently re-derived is a much better as-is than as-is, trust us — but a risk function still has to accept it, in writing.

At formation, nothing works

Until three verifiers are active, no artifact can reach full admission. An alliance that commissions work before recruiting verifiers will have paid for artifacts nobody can consume. Verifier recruitment is a launch prerequisite, and it is easy to mistake for a growth activity because the machinery looks complete without it.

Appendix B — The admission ruleset

The gate evaluates the ruleset in two passes, structural then semantic. It is enumerated in full in artifact-architecture §3.7, which is the only place the rules are numbered or counted. A count printed in prose drifts from the artifact it summarises, and this appendix drifted once already — it described the ruleset as it stood before advisory-record integrity was added.

The rules divide into groups. Signature and log validity covers envelopes, certificate chains, log inclusion and the witnessed checkpoint set. Verifier quorum requires k distinct registered verifiers with no dissent. Anchor re-derivability requires the baseline to resolve publicly, with a supplementary log witness in ecosystems that permit deletion. Graph and digest-binding integrity covers the unbroken chain back to that anchor. Contract conformance covers scope, corpus, proof completeness, exploitability status and the binary conformance verdict. Compile agreement has both sides compile the policy from the signed contract and compare digests, so a signed layout is verified rather than merely authenticated. Bundle freshness bounds the age of the trust material, since offline verification forfeits the trust root's own currency guarantee. And advisory-record integrity pins the vulnerability record each scope entry cites at commissioning and digests it as carried, so the affected range the contract asserts is checkable rather than the author's word.

Every rule must be decidable from the evidence bundle alone. A rule requiring a live lookup is either wrong or evidence of a missing bundle element, and that test is what keeps the hermeticity claim falsifiable rather than aspirational.
